A river does most of its work during floods. When the water rises, it carries sand and gravel that scrape the bed and widen the banks, and a single season can move more rock than a decade of calm flow.

Over thousands of years the channel settles into a shape that balances the slope of the land against the amount of sediment it must carry. Geologists call this a graded profile, and you can see it in the gentle curve of most old valleys.

columns: A short essay on slow colonists

Lichens are partnerships between a fungus and an alga, and the arrangement is older than most of the forests that now shelter them. Neither partner could survive alone on bare stone, but together they build a crust that holds water and gathers dust from the passing wind.

Because they grow so slowly, lichens record the age of the surfaces they cover. Researchers measure the width of the largest patches on gravestones of known date and use the results to estimate how long a glacier has been retreating from a valley floor.

They are also sensitive to the air. Many species disappear where sulphur dioxide is common, so a careful survey of the bark of street trees tells a city more about its pollution than a handful of expensive monitoring stations.
The next time you pass an old wall, look closely at the grey and orange rosettes on its stones. Each one has been growing there for decades, patiently turning rock into the first thin layer of soil.
photo: Every evening at dusk the keeper climbed the spiral stairs, counted the one hundred and twelve steps, and trimmed the wick before the light was lit. He kept a small notebook in his coat pocket and wrote down the colour of the sky.
In winter the storms came in from the west and the glass rattled in its frame. On those nights he did not sleep at all, but sat beside the lamp with a cup of strong tea and listened to the sea.
When the supply boat finally arrived in April, the captain found the notebook full and asked if he could read it.
